title: How Did Craft Beer Catch On? | Market Inventors
excerpt: Snow and Tsingtao are giving way to Jing-A, Slow Boat, Panda Brew and abbey ales.
body:
Snow and Tsingtao, our everyday beers, are giving way to Jing-A, Slow Boat, Panda Brew and abbey ales.

If you happen to be in Beijing, try a partial craft beer tour of the city's east side.

Start at No. 4 Gongti North Road, where an industrial-style beer bar has the word "Jing-A" mounted on a dark red brick wall. Then head northwest to Wudaoying, by the Second Ring Road. In this narrow hutong a small storefront sells beers called "Panda Brew." Next door is a live music venue called School, where you can try "Harvest," a beer brewed in Chengdu. From Wudaoying, turn left and go west into Jianchang Hutong, where a converted bungalow serves four house-brewed beers: "Pilgrim's Progress," "Blackout," "Golden Armor" and "Jianchang Stout." All are above 4% alcohol by volume, and, as you might guess, "Blackout" is the strongest. If you are still sober, head south to the "Slow Boat Fresh Beer Bar" in Dongsi, or east to "Great Leap Brewing" on Xinyuan Street.

In Shanghai, you can put together the same kind of crawl.

Tap House, Boxing Cat, Shanghai Brewery and Dr. Beer all sell their own beers. At Daga Brew Pub, on Tai'an Road at Xingguo Road, you can drink single-batch beers from small brewers around the country. And at Jiugui Canteen, "Jack's Dimple" and the "Haifu Convenience Store," which claims the widest range of imported beers in Shanghai, you can buy imported bottles such as Belgium's Westvleteren abbey beer and Britain's BrewDog.

![A craft beer bar](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031253534bnvRcBqwsJU0uHV.jpg-w600)

Craft beer's sudden arrival over the past year or two, and the drinkers behind it, look like a chicken-and-egg story: we cannot tell which drove which. What we can tell is that the rows of shops, the craft beer vocabulary on WeChat Moments and, more to the point, real purchases are turning up more and more often.

Craft beer really does seem to have caught on.

"The idea of craft beer has existed in the Chinese market for roughly five to ten years. But it has only really taken off in the past year or two," Zhang Yi, a senior beverage analyst for China at the market research firm Mintel, told QDaily. In a report Mintel finished at the end of last year, 18% of consumers said they had drunk craft beer. That is still largely a niche, but it is far above the firm's expectation of under 5%.

### Craft beer has no clear definition, and that vagueness helps it spread

"I think we differ from the industrial beer on the market in four ways: our ingredients are fine; we never lower our standards to cut costs; we don't use additives that dull the flavor; and unlike most industrial beers, which are bottom-fermented lagers, ours are top-fermented ales," Pan Dinghao, founder of Panda Brew, told QDaily.

Panda Brew was founded in 2013 and now runs two bars in Beijing, in Wudaoying Hutong and at Beixinqiao. It sells more bottled beer than any other domestic craft brand and is one of only two local craft brands of its kind, the other being Master Gao in Nanjing. Consumers in more than 40 Chinese cities can buy its two bottled beers locally.

![Pan Dinghao, founder of Panda Brew](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125354LH621w8enYEKdTmj.jpg-w600)

Pan Dinghao, founder of Panda Brew

When Pan Dinghao says "I think" and Zhang Yi says consumers "believe" they have drunk it, you can probably guess that neither producers nor consumers are sure what the industry's standards are.

"Craft beer" is a new term in Chinese. In English it is usually "craft beer," and the opposite of this word, with its hint of devotion to craftsmanship, is "industrial beer," or "watery beer," which generally means the Tsingtao, Yanjing and similar brands we see on the dinner table.

From Pan Dinghao's account, you come away with an impression that sounds impressive but is hard to pin down: craft beer is a cut above in its ingredients and in how it tastes, and beer as the brewer understands it ought to be somewhat classier than the usual stuff. Beyond that, there seem to be no hard standards.

The American craft beer market, whose share rose from just 5% in 2010 to 11% last year, looks considerably more mature than China's. There, the Brewers Association (BA) has a more authoritative definition. First, annual output cannot exceed 6 million barrels (702,000 tonnes). Second, no more than 25% of the brewery can be owned by a non-craft brewer or other company. Third, most of the beer's flavor must come from traditional or innovative ingredients and fermentation.

But even the BA's standard changes with circumstances. Britain, whose beer culture is as strong as America's or stronger, has no comparable output limit, so such a limit is not an inevitable result of craft brewing's growth. And in some places, purists with an almost obsessive devotion to small-scale brewing believe that only the obscure and the niche count as craft.

![Craft beer glasses](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031253545ztORyWmQb7IjhFS.jpg-w600)

"Only if you truly know how to enjoy beer will you really understand what craft beer is. But if you are not that expert, whatever satisfies you can count as craft. In fact, every producer's and every consumer's idea of craft is very vague," Zhang Yi said.

With no clear definition, the label covers a great deal of ground, and plenty of murky water. To some extent this has made craft beer far more likely to be talked up, and so far more likely to be passed around and sold.

### Selling craft beer as a classier lifestyle and culture matters a great deal

From July 26 to August 1, Enjoy, the food app owned by Fanben, ran a special sale called "Craft Beer Showcase." Its list featured 24 craft beers, including Westvleteren 12 from Saint Sixtus in Belgium and La Trappe Quadrupel from the Netherlands. These beers are fairly obscure, but each comes with an appealing story, and phrases such as "limited output," "rigorous craftsmanship" and "rich flavor" come up again and again. Behind them, of course, comes a matching price.

"67% of people link the quality of the ingredients with whether a beer is premium, and nearly half think craft beer means premium," Zhang Yi said.

Mintel's figures show that craft beer drinkers generally have higher incomes. That also means where they live matters little. First-tier cities differ little from second- and third-tier cities: once people reach that level of spending, they buy. Meanwhile, e-commerce sites that stock craft beer have made buying it possible.

![Craft beer bottles](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125355Zu29oQBqRxaNFfVY.jpg-w600)

Besides premium, craft beer is linked with two other things: lifestyle and culture.

On July 19, a custom edition of Panda Brew with a redesigned label appeared at the launch event of 700 Bike. Last year, Panda Brew did a similar collaboration with Qyer.com. "It makes sense to work with brands that share a similar lifestyle," Pan Dinghao told QDaily.

Beyond these partner brands with a similar feel, competitors entering the field have also sped up the industry's growth. After Panda, brands such as Jing-A, Slow Boat, Boxing Cat and Harvest began appearing in cities across the country. Beijing and Shanghai each now have a craft beer association, along with craft beer festivals run by the associations or by the brands. "When everyone builds up momentum together, the culture spreads," Pan Dinghao said.

When Panda Brew started out, fewer than five brands in China were doing similar business, and more than half its customers were foreigners. Now most are Chinese. "Craft beer is part of a more advanced culture abroad, so it makes sense for foreigners to be the ones to bring it in," said Pan Dinghao, who studied automotive engineering in Canada, where he first tasted craft beer, and who puts great weight on the cultural role of the Western context. In his view, most of the Chinese who founded the first craft beer brands had overseas experience like his. And besides Panda, brands such as Jing-A and Slow Boat were founded by foreigners living in China.

Panda Brew regularly imports craft beer styles that domestic brewers lack the ability to make, or cannot make quickly. Every Wednesday, Pan Dinghao brings these beers out for a "Panda Selects Tasting" in the shop. "It is a way of educating people, so they know what really good beer tastes like." The tastings brought Pan Dinghao and Panda Brew frequent media coverage, which in turn drew in both beer lovers and the merely curious. In this way, an event that moves from product to socializing helped beer lovers find their place within the scene, and, through its tie to lifestyle, drew in more outsiders.

Still, while craft beer culture is in its early days, spreading it through shops alone only goes so far. That is why Panda changed course in the summer of 2013. Before, it sold only draft beer in its own shop; after, it also began selling bottles. Having placed its draft beer in bars and shops in more than 40 cities through local distributors, it set the price at 20-40 yuan. "In a bar, the price should be one everyone can afford, and you get to drink better beer, so why not?" Pan Dinghao said.

Craft beer works like a tag that shows off personality. Getting consumers to know it, to want to buy it and to be labeled by it: these are the dividends that marketing craft culture can bring.

### More and more people care about taste over brand, which is another opening for craft beer

It is no longer news that craft beer poses a growing threat to industrial beer. Not long ago, the Irish brand Guinness imitated craft brewers with an ad focused on brewing craft and taste, which is clear evidence of that.

According to a report by the market research firm Euromonitor, China's Snow beer alone accounted for 5.4% of global beer sales, making it the world's most-drunk beer brand. In May this year, Zeng Shenping, marketing president of Snow Beer, said the beer market's next growth will come from the countryside; in other words, the breadth and depth of the Chinese market are enough to give Snow its huge base. In first-tier cities, by contrast, the market is quietly changing.

"In our survey, 77% of consumers who have drunk beer think taste matters more than brand. This trend is quietly helping craft beer," Zhang Yi told QDaily.

According to the China Alcoholic Drinks Association, China's beer output and sales in 2014 came to 4921.9 KL, down 0.96% year on year, the first decline in 24 years. More and more people are getting picky about how their beer tastes.

![A glass of craft beer](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031253560RzG28lcjXQhT9wx.jpg-w600)

One view that runs through Pan Dinghao's remarks is that this generation has never drunk really good beer, and so settles, with no real choice, for industrial beer. In practice, he deliberately adjusts the taste toward "Chinese characteristics." "We think Chinese people like lower bitterness and more sweetness, or a taste that is middle-of-the-road in every respect." So Panda Brew added wildflower honey to one of its beers, a honey beer, to bring the bitterness down to a level most people can accept.

This attention to taste is both a friendly gesture and an opportunity, both pandering and education. In short, more and more city dwellers have money, free time and a taste for better things, and all of this has made craft beer's growth possible.

"Consumers are ready for craft beer," Zhang Yi said.

### Beer giants have already swallowed some craft brewers. Will craft beer stay what it is now?

If craft beer is what happens once industrial beer reaches a certain stage, then its rise is a case of the times making the hero rather than the hero making the times: an outcome with an element of chance, since without craft the market might have gone another way. At the same time, just as the beer industry was bound to evolve, there is something inevitable about craft beer's arrival.

Since 2008, total sales of America's thousands of craft beer brands have jumped 80%. Of a US beer market worth about US$101.5 billion in 2014, craft beer already accounted for US$19.6 billion. But in this older market, several lengths ahead of China's, we see another kind of change. By 2011, AB InBev, America's largest brewer, had already bought four craft brewers, including Chicago's Goose Island Brewing.

![Craft beer taps](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125356XDzwbpf1AId5xV0o.jpg-w600)

For these craft brewers, dealing with capital has always been a trade-off. The beer may get worse as a result, but no longer worrying about money may give a brand more room to focus on brewing. Still, there are always skeptics: once big brewers start paying attention to this market and buying their way in, is craft beer still the craft beer it used to be?

The craft beer boom we see today more or less reflects the beer market's evolution. But evolution happens in stages, and the moment when craft beer goes mass-market is sure to come.
